newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends down vs. yen as negative comments continue.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends down vs. yen as negative comments continue.

text.p: The dollar fell against the Japanese yen Tuesday as three Japanese economic officials called for a halt to the dollar's recent rally.

Those comments came just one day after a Japanese finance ministry official had triggered heavy dollar sales with similar remarks and reinforced market perceptions that Japan might act to slow the pace of the dollar's ascent.
"It's quite clear the Japanese are trying to talk a top to the dollar right now and it's beginning to affect our markets," said Stephen Flanagan, senior foreign exchange dealer at Credit Agricole.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka at a news conference in Tokyo warned that "an excessively weak or strong yen is not favourable for the Japanese economy".
He added: "We want exchange rates to stabilise."
Later in Tokyo, top officials of Japan's Economic Planning Agency and Trade Ministry made similar statements, helping to keep the dollar on the defensive.
The dollar fell to 115.19 yen from 115.77 late Monday.
Against most other currencies, the dollar ended little changed from Monday's levels.
The dollar was nearly unchanged at 1.5637 German marks from 1.5640 and 1.3535 Swiss francs versus 1.3537.
The British pound rose modestly to $1.6950 from $1.6935. The dollar slipped to Canadian $1.3567 from C$1.3652.
Late in U.S. trade, the dollar was again hit by negative comments -- this time from Gail Fosler, chief economist at the Conference Board, a private economic research firm.
Fosler told an audience in Washington that the dollar was 15 percent overvalued against the yen, fuelling a brief flurry of dollar selling, dealers said.
The dollar slipped to just below 115 yen on the news before bargain-hunters emerged to bolster the currency.

"The Conference Board is just an independent group, but the dollar has been trading heavily for the last couple of days, so it was poised for some retracement on a comment like that," said Russell Lascala, chief spot trader at Citibank.
Heavy losses in the Japanese stock market helped offset the dollar's weakness against the yen. The Nikkei index of 225 stocks fell 2.83 percent, discouraging would-be yen buyers.
"People don't generally want to buy the currency of a country whose financial markets are getting destroyed," said Seth Garrett, director of foreign exchange at CS First Boston.
Market players also remained dubious that Japan would back up its verbal assault on the dollar with actual open market purchases of yen for dollars.
A weaker yen makes Japanese products more competitively priced in global markets and Japan will likely not act to stop a gradual dollar climb, dealers said.
"I still believe the comments out of Japan were aimed at the pace of the (dollar) move rather than the direction," Garrett said.
